title: Electrodynamics
tagline: Maxwell’s equations as a working theory
summary: Electrostatics and magnetostatics as boundary-value problems, Maxwell’s equations, waves in vacuum and in matter, radiation, and the fields of moving charges.
overview: The integral laws of the second-year course are Maxwell's theory seen from outside. This course goes inside. The same four equations are written as differential equations, solved as boundary-value problems, and used to compute the fields of realistic charges and currents, the energy and momentum those fields carry, the waves they radiate, and the way they look to a moving observer.

The course begins with statics. Electrostatics becomes Poisson's equation with boundary conditions: the uniqueness theorem is proved, and images, separation of variables in Cartesian and spherical coordinates, and the multipole expansion are developed as methods, with dielectrics treated through bound charge and $\mathbf D$. Magnetostatics follows the same plan with the vector potential, gauge freedom, the magnetic dipole, and magnetised matter described by $\mathbf H$. Maxwell's displacement current then unifies the two; Poynting's theorem and the Maxwell stress tensor show that energy and momentum live in the field; and the Lorenz gauge turns the equations into wave equations for the potentials. The second half applies them: reflection and refraction, skin depth, plasmas and waveguides; retarded potentials, the Liénard–Wiechert fields, the Larmor formula, antennas and the blue sky; and finally the field tensor $F^{\mu\nu}$, the transformation of $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$, and the field of a moving charge.

The calculations are longer than in the first electromagnetism course, and the physics is in the boundary conditions and the choice of gauge as much as in the algebra. Before choosing coordinates, write down the symmetry of the problem and the boundary data in a sentence; after finishing, check the answer against a limit you already know (a point charge, a conductor, $v \ll c$). Every number in the lessons can be reproduced with a calculator and CODATA constants, and doing so is the best way to learn the orders of magnitude.
outcomes: Prove the uniqueness theorem for Poisson's equation and use it to justify solutions found by images or by inspection.
Solve electrostatic boundary-value problems by images and by separation of variables in Cartesian and spherical coordinates, using Fourier and Legendre series.
Compute multipole moments of charge and current distributions and the dipole fields they produce, and explain why there is no magnetic monopole term.
Use bound charges and currents, $\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf H$, and the interface conditions to find fields in linear dielectric and magnetic media.
Derive the displacement current, Poynting's theorem and the Maxwell stress tensor from Maxwell's equations, and use them to compute energy flow, momentum and forces.
Work with the scalar and vector potentials in the Coulomb and Lorenz gauges, and carry out gauge transformations.
Derive the Fresnel coefficients and Brewster's angle, and compute skin depths, plasma frequencies and waveguide cutoffs for real materials and devices.
Derive the Larmor formula and the power and pattern of electric dipole radiation, and apply them to antennas and to Rayleigh and Thomson scattering.

Write Maxwell's equations in covariant form, transform $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ between inertial frames, use the invariants $\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf B$ and $E^2 - c^2B^2$, and find the field of a uniformly moving charge.

chapters.title: Electrostatics as a boundary-value problem

chapters.title: Magnetostatics
chapters.summary: The vector potential, Ampère’s law in differential form, and magnetic multipoles.

chapters.title: Maxwell’s equations
chapters.summary: The differential equations, gauges, the continuity equation, and energy and momentum in the field.

chapters.title: Waves in matter
chapters.summary: Dielectrics, conductors, reflection and refraction, and waveguides in outline.

chapters.title: Radiation
chapters.summary: Retarded potentials, dipole radiation, and the power radiated by an accelerated charge.

chapters.title: Fields of moving charges
chapters.summary: The Liénard–Wiechert potentials and the transformation of E and B.

history.title: The inverse-square law
history.detail: Charles-Augustin de Coulomb measured the force between charged spheres with a torsion balance and established that it falls as the inverse square of the distance.

history.title: Currents make magnetic fields
history.detail: Hans Christian Ørsted saw a current deflect a compass needle; within months Biot and Savart measured the field of a wire and Ampère began the study of forces between currents that he summarised in 1826.

history.title: Green's essay
history.detail: George Green's privately printed essay on electricity and magnetism introduced the potential function, Green's identities and the Green's-function method for boundary-value problems.

history.title: Electromagnetic induction
history.detail: Michael Faraday discovered that a changing magnetic flux induces a current, and pictured the space around charges and magnets as filled with lines of force.

history.title: A dynamical theory of the field
history.detail: James Clerk Maxwell, having introduced the displacement current in 1861–62, presented the complete field equations in 1865 and identified light as an electromagnetic wave; his Treatise followed in 1873.

history.title: Energy flow in the field
history.detail: John Henry Poynting derived the theorem on the flux of electromagnetic energy; Oliver Heaviside, who found it independently, recast Maxwell's equations in the four-equation vector form in 1884–85.

history.title: Electromagnetic waves detected
history.detail: Heinrich Hertz generated and detected electromagnetic waves with spark-gap dipoles in 1887–88, measuring their reflection, refraction and polarisation.

history.title: The field of a moving charge
history.detail: Alfred-Marie Liénard (1898) and Emil Wiechert (1900) derived the potentials of a point charge in arbitrary motion, following Joseph Larmor's 1897 formula for the power radiated by an accelerated charge.

history.title: The electrodynamics of moving bodies
history.detail: Building on Lorentz's transformations (1892–1904), Albert Einstein derived them from the relativity principle and the constancy of the speed of light, and gave the transformation of E and B between frames.

history.title: The field tensor
history.detail: Hermann Minkowski reformulated electrodynamics in four-dimensional spacetime and wrote the electromagnetic field as a single antisymmetric tensor.

references.title: Introduction to Electrodynamics
references.note: Fifth edition. The standard upper-level text and the closest companion to this course, with excellent worked problems on boundary-value problems, radiation and relativistic fields.

references.title: Electricity and Magnetism
references.authors: Edward M. Purcell and David J. Morin
references.note: Third edition. The best place to build physical intuition, especially its derivation of magnetism from relativity and its treatment of fields in matter.

references.title: Modern Electrodynamics
references.note: A rich, modern text bridging the undergraduate and graduate levels, with careful physical discussion and many applications; good for dielectrics, waveguides and radiation.

references.title: Classical Electrodynamics
references.note: Third edition. The graduate reference: Green's functions, multipoles, waveguides, radiation and the relativistic theory in full.

references.title: The Classical Theory of Fields
references.authors: L. D. Landau and E. M. Lifshitz
references.note: Course of Theoretical Physics, vol. 2, fourth English edition. A concise, relativistic-first treatment of the field tensor, invariants, the fields of moving charges and radiation.

references.title: Electromagnetism (lecture notes)
references.note: Cambridge lecture notes, freely available. A clear path through the undergraduate theory, with a good chapter on the relativistic formulation.
